utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today. Judge Prost and Judge Stole are unable to attend. I notice from amongst the accused, Beara is absent today. Perhaps, Mr. Ostojic, you would like to address that matter with the Trial Chamber. Do we have a waiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. We do not have a waiver physically. We do have an oral waiver. We spoke to Mr. Beara. We were with him last night from 6.00 to 8.00. He was not feeling well and there was no staff really available for us to communicate that immediately, and we just weren't sure this morning. Now we know that he's not going to arrive, and it's forthcoming, the waiver. It should be here before the close of our session today, so I anticipating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for your kindness, Mr. Beara -- Mr. Ostojic. So also for the record, the Prosecution is represented by Mr. -- wait, wait, because I have got some preliminaries. For the record, the Prosecution is represented today by Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Soljan. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, and I think that's it. All right. There are some matters we would like to raise with you, this being probably the last day we are meeting before the recess. Late yesterday evening, we received another motion from the Nikolic Defence team, seeking leave to add one witness to his Rule 65 ter list. We would like to know if the Prosecution is in a position to respond to this motion now. In it, accused Nikolic seeks leave to add a witness that the Defence met for the first time in early June of this year. The submission is that both the co-accused and the Prosecution will have ample time and opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We know that, as such, the motion in itself is not urgent, because the Defence of Mr. Nikolic is not going to start tomorrow, but still, I mean, the earlier we decide this, the more time you have to prepare yourselves. Perhaps we could leave it until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is the first I've heard, but Mr. Nicholls is here and we'll have him look at it. I mean, he's here today, and we'll have him look at it and be able to advise me at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Also, the Nikolic Defence team filed two motions in the last few days, seeking protective measures, protective measures of various kinds. Again, if we have your response, we could perhaps dispose of these two motions in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I am aware of those, and we are working on those. And I will get back to you on the break on those as well. I'm hopeful we can get those done before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, especially the one seeking delay of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I know we're going to be objecting to that and it should be a simple objection, I hope, and so I want to get that to you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And then you will recall that some time back earlier on this month, basically in the beginning, 4th of July, the Miletic Defence team filed a motion seeking instructions regarding interviews conducted by other parties of witnesses on the Miletic witness list. The essence of the motion was a request to the Trial Chamber to instruct all parties, Prosecution and co-accused alike, to notify the Miletic Defence team of their intention to interview the witnesses on the Miletic witness list, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G), and if a witness refuses to be interviewed, to respect the decision of that particular witness or witnesses. We have had two responses to that, one from the Pandurevic Defence team that takes no position. The same approach was taken by the Prosecution in its 16 July response. On the 17th, the Gvero Defence team also replied, saying that they took no position on the merits. However, they questioned the competence of this Trial Chamber to decide on the matter. You know that such like issues have arisen not only in other cases but also in this case, albeit involving Prosecution witnesses rather than Defence witnesses, and you also know that there is nothing written in the Rules, probably mainly due to the fact that these belong more to the area or fall more in the area of odontological or ethical behaviour, rather than rules. There are two options, and the first preference is for us to invite you to discuss this amongst yourselves and come to an agreement, the same way we did when, earlier on, we had the same question arising involving the possible interviews of Prosecution witnesses. Only then we did give you some indication of what we believe is the ideal or what is the way that you should deal with these issues. And considering that there has been no objection to -- formal objection to Madame Fauveau's motion, perhaps again the best way to go about it is to have a roundtable, and anyone who wishes to interview Madame Fauveau's witnesses, or any or all of them, would better sit down and discuss on the protocol. However, we can tell you that what we consider to be the system or the protocol that you should be aiming at; namely, any one of you, referring to everyone here who wishes to interview a witness on the Miletic witness list, should notify the Miletic Defence team of such an intention. In other words, it should not be done behind the back of the Miletic Defence team. The second protocol maxim that we had indicated to you was that if a witness declines -- refuses to be interviewed, then his or her decision should be respected. This you will find also written down in decisions of this Tribunal. I mean, I could refer you to a decision of mine or my team in Oric and also another decision in the Mrksic case. So, more or less, that should be the -- what should inspire you as to the way you should be acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, there is one final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There is two final things. One is: You were supposed yesterday -- by yesterday, Mr. Ostojic, to file -- or Monday, in relation to the Prosecution motion, we had set a deadline which expired yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm familiar with that, and we did file something late last night. We were in the prison, and when we got back, we finished it. We attached an annex, and we set out exactly what our position is on those three or four points that were raised. I think two of them were actually discussed with the OTP a couple days ago. We reached an accord on those. It's reflected in the motion. You should be getting it this morning at some time, if you haven't already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, have you seen this filing or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not yet, but as you know, there is a Registry delay sometimes. We appreciate courtesy copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: that short of an agreement between you two, we will have to hand down a decision which might hurt, and that decision would need to be issued by this Friday, at the latest. That's tomorrow. So what I am suggesting is Madam Registrar will check with the Registry what's happened to this filing, have a quick copy of it sent upstairs here, or downstairs, or across - I don't know - and if you could kindly come back to us during -- or after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. No problem, Mr. President. And the 65 ter motion of Nikolic, I now do remember that, discussing that with Mr. Nicholls, and I don't think that's going to be a problem. But I'll get back to you definitively at the break on that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. The last, and it has given us quite some -- quite a few problems to decide. However, I agree with -- we agree with Ms. Fauveau that barring a few exceptions here and there, we have moved or conducted -- managed to conduct this trial so far in a positive manner, and more or less to our satisfaction, although we would have preferred if things were -- had speeded up more. But our experience with you has been that we found your words more or less were to be trusted, and when you promised that extra time would translate into more efficiency and a shorter case, that seems to have worked fine. We have -- although we are not in perfect harmony ourselves on this, we are not unanimous on this, we are agreeing that if we give you the -- if we start on the 25th of August instead of the 20th of August, it will be to everyone's benefit. The understanding is those of you who've still got to prepare for their defence will try to utilise these few days - we're talking of including Saturday and Sunday, we're talking of five days, so we're not talking of much - but it gives you basically a week within which to organise yourselves even better and perhaps reduce further your defence cases. We'll be sitting on the afternoon of the 25th, afternoon of the 25th. Although it's a Monday, we're sitting in the afternoon because of arrangements we had to make with others. All right. So we'll come back to other issues after the break. Madam Usher, if you could kindly bring in the witness, please. Let's try and finish with this witness at the earliest possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to make an effort to finish you off as early as possible. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and I'll do my best to contribute to this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Radovanovic. I don't know if you've had an opportunity to get some rest, because we had extended hours yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you recall where we stopped yesterday. I read the transcript, and I noticed that the last topic that we were dealing with was the analysis of 4D535, and I was explaining the four criteria that the Borovcanin Defence was guided in producing it. Do you need me to repeat the four criteria?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember them, so you don't have to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now that you've had an opportunity to look at this document, of course you can confirm that what is identical for all the persons on the list is that the grave-site in Glogova is the place where all of them were found?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what we can see on the list is that all the persons from this list meet at least one of the remaining three criteria; namely, that the exact date of their disappearance is not known or that it is after the 13th, rather, and that the place where they disappeared is at some distance from the farming co-op in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there are some dates that precede the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you. So only one of the three criteria. So we have one that is common to all, the Glogova grave-site, and at least one of the remaining three criteria have been met?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And of course you can confirm, although it is quite obvious, that there are 95 persons listed here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we can now go into private session. I will just ask about a couple of entries on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. I take it there are no further cross-examinations from the Defence teams, which means I can now ask Madam Soljan from the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to us and good afternoon to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Feels like the afternoon, Your Honours, already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Lada Soljan, for the record. I am a member of the Prosecution team in this case. Now, we haven't met before, that's right, and we haven't discussed this case in the past?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we haven't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, just before we get into the subject matter and the questions I have for you, I wanted to double-check something. In your report, you listed on the last two pages of it the 22 sources, reports, that you looked at in compiling your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And among those documents that I saw there, there were -- you listed the six sources that had been used by the OTP demographers, the OTP experts. They were the seven sources that you also list in your report, six reports that were issued by Helge Brunborg and other demographers, two articles, and a report by Dean Manning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it's correct. As soon as I have listed them, it must be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just a clarification, please. Under number 7, you had listed a document called "List of Exhumed and Identified Persons, Srebrenica Region, ICMP Identified DNA List." Could you just clarify for me what that list was, exactly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of my work, on several occasions I received seven or eight versions of these lists, and that's why I did not list the versions precisely. The versions were very different. I had an occasion to see versions that were disclosed by the OTP, i.e., letters that were sent by individuals from the International Commission for the Identification of Persons sent to the demography department. In other words, I saw versions relative and ranging in numbers from 4.000 something, and I can't tell you the exact numbers, 5.000 something, 8.000 something, and even 10.000 something. I can't give you the precise numbers to give you at the moment, but I have those in the witness room. I have two versions that I can show you in hard copy. To sum it up, I've seen several versions of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when you were looking at them, were they in Excel spreadsheet format or did you get hard copies of them, or Excel spreadsheets that were on a CD?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was in hard copy. However, what I do, everything is in hard copy. I did my all -- all printing in order to be able to carry out some comparisons and in order to arrive at a complete picture. In other words, I never received anything in hard copy. Whatever I have in hard copy is the printed versions of the material disclosed by the OTP which I printed by myself. When I work, I always use -- I always scribble on the margins, make my little notes, and that makes my work easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you understood where this data, the one that you call list of exhumed and identified persons, where it originated?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The origin is the demographic department of the OTP, that's the origin. I don't have any other sources of lists that I might have received from the Commission. All the documents originated from the OTP. But based on some note of correspondence, I could see where they had come from. There was correspondence about corrections, about possible numbers, possible suggestions, and so on and so forth. That's part of the correspondence attached to those lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I think I may not have been clear enough when I was asking the question. What I meant was: This document that you list as ICMP-identified DNA lists, do you know what that source of that data is? Who created that list or those lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I could conclude from reading different documents, this was done by the International Commission for Identification, and the lists contain certain interventions, and I don't mean corrections, but certain conclusions about people who were identified, who were not, who were still missing, and this was done by the expert demographers of the OTP in The Hague. There are several lists. There's one which provides the names of the persons and the DNA identification. You can see those. There's a lot of duplicates because a lot of re-association was done. Later on, you have the same lists, but then the demographic department had compared them with the lists of missing and dead and conclude that some persons are still missing, some were identified, and so on and so forth. The way I understood it is that the authors of those lists were from the International Commission for Identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you're aware, Madam, that OTP experts considered it as a primary source to be used together with the ICRC and the PHR lists in the establishment of this -- of the new progress report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to define or clarify the meaning of a primary source. In what terms can something be a primary source? What did they use in order to establish who was identified? Is that the meaning of a primary source, as you use it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: "Primary source" in the sense in which, I think they -- they also used it -- in which Helge Brunborg used it when he was testifying as well, in the sense that the ICRC and the PHR lists were his primary source, and he was now considering ICMP as a third primary source in putting together the list of missing unidentified persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm objecting only because I don't think my learned friend answered the doctor's question as to how she defines "primary source." She just said Dr. Brunborg utilised it as a primary source, but I think the witness is asking for clarification as to what constitutes a primary source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't actually -- I don't think I need to be clarifying this. I just -- I think "primary source" is a pretty clear -- it's being discussed in all of Mr. Brunborg's reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think everyone knows what a primary source is, as distinct from a secondary one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: But I can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, I would like to say something. Irrespective of the interpretation of the term "primary," in my report I say under item 6 that I also use data on the exhumed unidentified persons, and they can be obtained only from the International Commission of the Red Cross. Whether Mr. Brunborg used those directly or not, I can't say, but I know that one of the co-authors, Ms. Ewa Tabeau, compiled her list of 7.661 persons, and on the margin or on the side she made her remark -- she put her remark: "Identified," "still missing," and so on and so forth. I can't claim that this was done by Mr. Brunborg and that he had requested that, but he does mention that source in his report and that's why I listed it. Whether it was a primary source to Mr. Brunborg or not, I wouldn't know, because he did not dwell upon it, and he did not go into the greatest of details in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: In fact, I would beg to differ, in his direct examination he actually specifically referred to it as his primary source, but I'll move on. When you were preparing your expert report and your testimony for this week, did you review any other testimony beyond Mr. Brunborg's?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand "any other testimony about that." About what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Any other related testimony in this case, any other testimony related to demography, related to graves, related to the events of Srebrenica, any testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed Dr. Brunborg's testimony. I was present at his cross-examination. I observed Dr. Ewa Tabeau's testimony and also the testimony of Dr. Mladen Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you also have a chance to review the report of Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: But you haven't seen or followed or read the testimony of Dr. Thomas Parsons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Thomas Parsons and the recording of his testimony I did not see, but I read his letters to Ewa Tabeau about identification and about reaching a certain number of identified persons eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you didn't follow the testimony of Mr. Dean Manning, either, did you, or read it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only read Mr. Dean Manning's reports. I did not read the transcript of his testimony, nor did I watch him providing his testimony. I read both reports by Dean Manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I cut you off. What you meant was, I presume, the June and November 2007 reports of Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be really precise, I have them on me and I can tell you which reports these are. One is June 2007, and the other is November 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And just additionally, did you listen to or read any of the testimony of the forensics experts, such as Jose Baraybar, John [sic] Haglund, John Clark, Richard Wright, or Christopher Lawrence, all of whom testified in 2007?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not listen to them, but I listened to some other forensic experts who did not testify in The Hague at this Tribunal, but rather at the court in Sarajevo. Again, the subject matter was the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Therefore, since you didn't review the testimonies of these individuals testifying in this current case, you also wouldn't have reviewed any of the documents they had produced, any of their experts reports, forensic expert reports; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the forensic experts that you mentioned just a while ago, no, I really did not peruse any of their expert reports. But I have to tell you something. The fact that I did not review their reports is nothing that I deemed very important or significant. I am interested in the possible number, and what the forensic experts think, it is not up to me to be the judge of what they think. What I did read was the detailed methodology for the identification of bodies, which includes DNA analysis and some bone analysis. I just wanted to have a rather broad picture of the methods used in the process of identifying missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, as you testified in the last few days here, your task was to study all the reports that were prepared by the OTP experts, to look at the sources that they used, to also consider other sources, and to come up with your own report, analysing all that data; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you take issue with the results reached by the OTP experts due to the sources that they use; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contest the methodology that the OTP experts used to arrive at the results that they have offered to this Court. I believe that the methodology is completely wrong, non-scientific, that it is not used anywhere else in the world but here at the Hague Tribunal, and I fully believe that such methodology is not capable of delivering reliable results.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: But your conclusion during your testimony, as well as how you lay it out in your report, isn't it, is that a part of the methodology is also the sources that you used, and you're saying more sources should have been used; the six sources that they'd been considering in their analysis were not sufficient?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably did not understand me correctly. The first step in the system called "methodology" is sources. Sources are part of any methodology and cannot be separated from it. The first step in methodology is the system of procedures to arrive at results. If your first step is wrong, you can be as good a methodologist as you may, but the result will always be problematic because of the erroneous first step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Whenever it's convenient to you, Ms. Soljan, we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can stop now and take it up in the next -- after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If we could get maybe five minutes before the next break, and Mr. Nicholls -- and we'll be able to deal with a couple of the issues very briefly that you brought up before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My idea, Mr. McCloskey, was to finish today's sitting during the next break, if Ms. Soljan can promise us to do that, leaving us five minutes or ten minutes. Do you think you can do that, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I will do my utmost, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Hi, again. So we were just speaking about the work you were doing and the work you were tasked to do by the Defence counsel. Just briefly, using your own criteria and the sources you analysed, what would your number of missing persons from Srebrenica be?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. In order to be able to say -- to give the accurate figure for the missing persons in Srebrenica, a lot of things have to be done. You have to be able to inspect some other sources. You have to know what Srebrenica is. You have to be sure that your sources are reliable. So I would not dare at all to say what, in my opinion, is the accurate figure for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you, yourself, did not try to put together a list of missing persons for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not my task, and that was not a task that I would accept in the current situation at this time. I would not be able to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Have you -- while disputing the methodology of the demographics experts of the OTP, have you taken any steps to confirm whether any individuals on the missing and dead list are, in fact, alive?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not my task, either. But your expert was able to determine, as early as in 2000, that there are nine such persons, and in 2005, well, I can't give you the exact information, but I think he determined that there were 20 something. And he used the strictest-possible method, and your expert did not present a probability, how many persons might still be determined to be alive had he used the 41st criterion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Madam, in the course of your testimony in the last few days, you've made a few highly-critical remarks about Mr. Brunborg and the work methodology of his team; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to stress that this has nothing to do with Mr. Brunborg as a person. I was critical of the expert and professional who applied the methodology that is improper in this manner. And let me underscore once again, Mr. Brunborg stated in his research -- he, himself, said in his study that this was unique methodology. This means that it has never been -- it had never been used before in any kind of scientific research.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So when you are calling the work being done as result driven, stating terms like "manipulation," "statistical exhibitionism," saying that he's looking for elements that suit his end result, that he would really like at any cost to find as many missing and dead as possible, doing something like that seems to imply dishonesty, that you're saying that he's dishonest; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with you. I don't know Mr. Brunborg, and I don't know whether he is an honest or a dishonest man. But I read his CV, and Mr. Brunborg graduated from great schools, highly-esteemed schools. He has been working in statistics bureau of Norway for years, and their statistics is one of the highly developed in Europe. So I really can't comprehend how Mr. Brunborg can apply certain methods in the way that he's done, and that's what I'm critical of. And now whether Mr. Brunborg is honest or dishonest, that has nothing to do with what I'm saying. He's just not doing this in a professionally-proper manner. Now, as to the reasons why he is doing that, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, at the end of the day, what this is all about is simply figuring out how many persons went missing or died after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Mr. Brunborg writes in his reports, he says that he was tasked by the Prosecution to determine the number of persons that went missing, and in the paper, The Genocide Count, he says that his task is to determine the number of persons killed by the army of Republika Srpska. So I'm just quoting from what Mr. Brunborg wrote, himself. So it was his task to determine the number of the missing and to confirm that they are, indeed, all of them dead, or at least to find some evidence to support the claim that they are all dead. And you can see that in the first report, the 2000 report, in the second report that he wrote in 2003, in the paper that he published and that is attached to the second report, and you can see that in 2005, he does not define the task, merely saying that he is updating the list. Now, in the list that Dr. Brunborg published in -- it's co-authored by Mr. Urdal, you can see the missing related to Srebrenica, that -- the army and so on, so from the forward to the 2000 list, you can see what Mr. Brunborg's task is, except on what you can conclude on the basis of the explanations he provides in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And the starting point for Dr. Brunborg's analysis, as you were able to find, was an analysis of the ICRC list of missing persons; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, I don't know what the starting point is. The term that was used in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: He looked at the ICRC missing list in order to determine how many individuals from this list are missing persons from Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, Dr. Brunborg did not analyse the ICRC list. Dr. Brunborg states that there is such a list and that missing persons are recorded there, the date when this work started, and he also states the number of persons on that list at the time when he is doing his first report, and he indicates how many versions of the list there were at the time when he started doing his job. So he did not analyse the ICRC list in the sense in which we, in our profession, understand an analysis to be. Dr. Brunborg analysed, to a limited extent, from my point of view, the data that he extracted from the ICRC list, on the basis of the date of disappearance, and regarding this analysis which is rather unilateral, because he analyses only his own data. You cannot have a comparative list when you're only comparing one thing with the same thing, so in this sense Dr. Brunborg did analyse the ICRC list, but only in this way that I just described. And I would just like to add, if I may - I apologise - that Dr. Brunborg, had he analysed this, he would have listed all the attributes that exist in the ICRC list that are not shown as attributes that Dr. Brunborg uses. In my opinion, if you analyse something, that means that you have to show everything that you have, everything that you can obtain from the ICRC raw material, to make an assessment and evaluation of the data that the ICRC has, and to emphasise some statistical deficiencies, indicating that you as a statistician, as a demographer, will do on -- will work on some of that, complying with all the statistical procedures, because the Red Cross is not bound by those procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, actually, since you mentioned the raw material, a few days ago you mentioned -- you were saying that you didn't know whether the OTP Demographics Unit ever attempted to get the raw data from the ICRC, and therefore that a major error was made precisely because we're not in possession of the raw material. But, in fact, Mr. Brunborg's testimony on May 9th, which you personally attended, he delineated precisely what data was made available and the fact that a request had been made, but that the ICRC, for neutrality purposes, was not able to honour that request, and therefore that the data that was possible was the basic data of names, father's name, last name, date of disappearance and place of disappearance, as reported by concerned family members. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Making a ten-line statement and just putting "isn't that correct" at the end of it doesn't make it a question. That isn't a question at all. It's quite simply a comment, and I don't know how the witness can be expected to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan, I think Mr. Haynes could be right this time. Do you think -- Doctor, do you think you can answer the question as phrased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question, if it was a question, was rather lengthy, but it is a fact that Dr. Brunborg, in the course of his examination - I don't know whether it was in chief or in cross - did say that from the ICRC raw material, the only thing that he saw was the questionnaire. There is a record of it. You can check. All the other attributes that Dr. Brunborg notes and all the things that he gathered that was in the cross-examination, it's just some of the attributes that are made public by the Red Cross. And I say that -- I state that with full responsibility. Now, is there raw material in the ICRC? Well, you can -- it is reasonable to conclude that if something was transferred from magnetic storage media, well, certainly there is raw material, because you couldn't do that just like that. Now, whether the Demographic Unit asked for those materials, I don't know. I don't have -- I didn't see any memos indicating that they wanted to get something and were not given it. But if the lead researcher says that the only thing that he saw was a blank questionnaire form, then I believe that those materials were never even sought.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, on 9th of May, 2007, in testimony - and this is at pages 1184 and 1185 - he was asked by Madam Nikolic: "Did you ask to get an insight into the questionnaire of the ICRC that served as basis for the ICRC list on their web site? Did you use the raw information from those questionnaires or did you just use the data from list?" "Yes, I think I've the questionnaire, an empty blank questionnaire, but as I told you just now, we did not get that other information. ICRC is very" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: " ... very protective about the information they are releasing, to preserve the neutrality so they have access to all sides in a conflict." Then Madam Nikolic continued to ask: "But did you ask for such information? Did you ask for that particular information in regard to every person reported as missing?" And Mr. Brunborg answered: "We made general requests for information, and I believe it was denied, but we could only get the information that had already been provided in electronic format. For example, there was also on the questionnaire they asked about ethnicity, which was not provided to us." So did you not hear this testimony, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it, and precisely on the basis of this question I based my conclusion that Dr. Brunborg may have asked for this material, but that he did not see a single questionnaire that had been filled in, and that Dr. Brunborg was happy with the electronic format that was given to him, and that perhaps he did not persist enough in his efforts to get it. But on the basis of what Dr. Brunborg said, that the justification that the ICRC decided to treat this material as confidential, is not logical enough. If the Red Cross places on the internet the first name, second name, date of birth, place of birth, father's name, and all the other -- or various other attributes, why would they conceal ethnicity or professional background? And if they thought that this material could not be posted on the internet, even if that were true, I can find it hard to believe that they would refuse to place this material at the disposal of an institution such as the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, just to read back the answer you just gave before giving me this rather long response, you said to my question regarding whether the raw material had been sought, you said: "Now, whether the Demographic Unit asked for those materials, I don't know. I don't see any memos indicating they wanted to get something. But if the lead researcher says that the only thing that he saw was" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, Ms. Soljan, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: " ... and I believe that those materials were never even sought."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Madam, which is it of those two?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure if I understand you correctly. You quote Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, you said that you believed that the materials were never sought. Did you or did you not hear his testimony saying that he sought the raw materials and did not receive them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. Without saying more in front of the witness, I think it mis-characterizes the testimony of Dr. Brunborg. And I think the witness did hear as it was given to her, and she's providing her answer based on that question. Now, my learned friend may have a different interpretation when Mr. Brunborg said that he generally asked for it, whether he generally assumed that because of neutrality, they may not give it. But if they have a document, and this cross-examination that any of the OTP experts, including Brunborg, asked for that specifically, they've never tendered it that I'm aware of, show it to the witness and we can move on on this issue rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've been carefully following what was going on, what the previous questions were, what the witness's previous answer was. Amongst other things that she said, that in her mind perhaps Mr. Brunborg was not persistent enough, but she continued to explain how, in her mind, also there seems to be a contradiction between what she knows and what he has stated. I think we can move ahead. We can move forward with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, are you really suggesting that the ICRC should be giving up this highly-sensitive data to any party that requests it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to suggest anything, Madam. I'm just trying to say that a lot of sensitive data was obtained at the request of the ICTY. Now, I really can't tell you, I don't whether the ICRC would be willing to give it or not, but I think that there is a lot of sensitive information right here, and you know that probably better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I don't think I quite understood that, but are you really -- are you basically saying that the ICRC should compromise its neutrality, especially in wartime situations such as these, out of which this kind of data arises?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're assuming that -- yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, and I think that the requests were made several years, if not many years after -- or should have been after the investigation of this case and during the trial. If they have a document that they asked for this documentation, they should show it to her. If they looked at the raw material, they should give us the documents that we asked for and were required to provide to us. Show it to the witness. It's cross-examination. It's not for this witness to say that Dr. Brunborg, based on his testimony, didn't look at that raw data. If she has evidence to counter that, they should bring it forth, and it's quite straight forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, Mr. Brunborg testified under oath about this issue. This was on cross-examination, and the Defence counsel had every opportunity at that time to ask for that raw data, if they were not satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, we do not carry the burden of proof. If they had that information pursuant to these Rules, they're required to provide it to us. If they're telling us now that Dr. Brunborg has that raw material, we invite them to produce it to us immediately. I don't think that's going to be their position, but this cat-and-mouse game really of shifting the burden of proof to us has got to stop. They're required to meet their burden. They are not doing it in this regard at all. If they don't have the documents to show this witness, I respectfully request that they move on on another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Really, what does it matter, what opinion this lady has as to whether the ICRC should disclose this material? Is it going to help you one bit with your judgement in this case? It's an utterly irrelevant question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Haynes. Ms. Soljan, will you move to your next area and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I will move to my next question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, a part of the analysis that Dr. Brunborg used, that the OTP experts used, in order to assemble their list of missing persons, was by taking the ICRC list and then, first of all, comparing it to the 1991 census; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we said yesterday. That's how Dr. Brunborg tried to prove that persons on his list were real people who actually existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you've already said that the 1991 census, the official, is not a perfect document; it contains errors?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that first names and last names were never checked. But generally speaking, the census in Bosnia and Herzegovina was evaluated as a success. This was not done by me. There is a procedure that is carried out when you want to declare whether a census is a success or not. So apart from the first and the last names that are not used as raw material for the census, and they're never checked, this census was a success. Of course, there are some questions where answers can be taken with some -- with a grain of salt because they're perhaps more or less reliable. And I would like to say something else. The moment you publish the census book, it means that the census was a success. There is not an institution dealing in statistics, the national statistics bureau, that would publish the census books with the results that are not considered to be good. If some attributes are considered to be bad, for instance, occupation, then no book is published regarding that attribute. So once the census books are published, it signals that the census was a success. Of course, we always have to look at what attribute this particular book is dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: But you'll agree with me that the 1991 census was not a 100 per cent complete document, listing all the individuals living in the former Yugoslavia at that time, or guest workers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not agree with you. What you say now, it's really something new for me. I wouldn't say that. In particular, if you're talking about the former Yugoslavia, the 1991 census was carried out in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. All the republics in the former Yugoslavia published some results based on the census. As far as I know, there is not a single republic in the former Yugoslavia that stated, "We are not going to publish this because it has not been a success." Of course, there are some attributes. Now, I don't know whether there's a census book for occupation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Maybe there is, but I haven't seen it. So there are some attributes that are not dealt with in books because they are not considered to be a success.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What I'm asking is: Not every single individual is listed in that list, not every person from every village has made it into the census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know where you get this information from, I really don't. There is a precise definition of the population, and if persons do not fall under the definition, they will not be entered. The population implies permanent residence, people who have a permanent address in the place where the census is taking place, irrespective of the fact whether the person is there or not at the moment when census is taken. There were a lot of people who were guest workers abroad, and they had been there for 5, 10, or 20 years. They were still part of the population of the former Yugoslavia, and during the moment of the census they were absent. And when I'm talking about the 1991, a lot of people arrived in different places to study there, work there, but they were not compromised in the census because they were not the permanent residents. Whether every single villager of every single village was compromised in the census, I can't tell you, but there is a check and double-check of the census subsequent to the census, in addition to all the checking that was done during the census-taking itself. And then it is this control that will tell you whether the census was, itself, successful or not. Who is it who can tell you whether every single person is accounted for? There may be major problems arising from totally illogical situations. For example, in one village you may have a thousand inhabitants and still you accounted for only 100 of them, but this is double-checked on the ground. Something else is then found as the reason for such an illogical thing. But in statistics, there is nothing illogical. Second of all, when you embark on a census, you don't just do it randomly, without any previous information. You have your estimates that are provided by the statistics, by a scientific methodology. You take into account natural flows in migrations. To cut a long story short, I can't claim that every single villager of every single village was accounted for, but I claim with full responsibility that the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina was successful because there was no single official institution in Bosnia and Herzegovina that issued a statement to the effect that what is being published is actually rubbish and should be taken with reservations. When I say that a census was successful, this does not mean that I should agree with the method and with the way things were done, but the statistics of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina are firmly behind the data, and this data therefore is official. I may criticise them as much as I can, taking certain features and characteristics into account, but I cannot -- I simply cannot ignore this reliable source of data.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Madam, the OTP experts found that 87 per cent of the names on the ICRC list matched against or were found on the 1991 census. You can agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was established using a lot of keys, and that's what they put in their report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And as was discussed yesterday, 1.030 persons did not match the 1991 census, were not found on the census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is stated in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you're suggesting that these 1.030 persons are fictitious, or you've even called them non-existent?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg says that when he defines his methodological procedure, and he says, and I quote: "In order for me to check whether certain persons are real or fictitious," because there had been objections about the published lists, "I matched the list" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What I was actually asking you -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, but what I was asking you was what you were saying yesterday, and you certainly had certainly mentioned non-existent persons.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, because the methodology used by Dr. Brunborg says whoever is not identified in the census does not exist. I may be paraphrasing it a bit wrongly, but I can quote, and he says to prove that somebody does exist, that he's not fictitious, "we matched with the census." And if your match result is 87 per cent, according to that methodology, then the remainder of the persons are not matched, so why should you keep them on the list? If that is your method for you to prove that somebody is alive or that they existed, then why would you still keep on your list something that you could not match and, thus, prove as ever having existed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And your suggestion, indeed, as you were saying yesterday, is it would be professionally correct to exclude these 1.030 persons from the OTP list of missing and dead persons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be professionally correct, to say the least, to emphasise -- to highlight that now you are dealing with certain individuals of whom you're not sure that they exist, rather than distribute these people mostly onto the territory of Srebrenica. There's no single statistical proof, according to Dr. Brunborg's methodology, for these people, so how does he know that most of them hail from Srebrenica, fewer of them from other places? How can he tell?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, are you basically suggesting, then, that all these Muslim families who were reporting these 1.030 persons as missing were lying to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam, not for a single moment did I say that Muslim families lied to the ICRC. What I'm saying is that Dr. Brunborg does not perform his job in a methodologically-proper way. The fact that he was not able to match about 1.030 persons doesn't mean that these people do not exist, these Muslims and their families. And what does it have to do with them, after all? In his table 5 or 6, Dr. Brunborg, in his report, he is not aware of the national background or ethnic background for 999 male. How does then, Madam Prosecutor, know that these were Muslims? And let me tell you exactly what table that is. It is on page -- on page 27 of the Serbian version. I wouldn't be able to point you to the English page. And please allow me to finish. Page 27 of Dr. Brunborg's report, drafted in 2005, table 7, he says "National and Sex Distribution of the Missing and Dead Person Related to Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's page 23 of the report, if you want to follow along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Brunborg provides a table with national and sex distribution. You will see there is 6.531 Muslim males, 37 females, and 6.568 in total. There are also Croats, Serbs and other ethnic backgrounds, but I would like to draw your attention to those whose ethnic background is not known. There's 999 of them, males, 31 females, or 1.031 persons in total whose ethnicity is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Well, one point I'd like to make is after you testified yesterday, I consulted with the Demographic Unit and asked them to just assemble the list of those 1.030 so-called fictitious persons and match it against the July list that we have just received from the ICMP, and it was disclosed to all the Defence and, I presume, to you, and the is that result 527 of the individuals you have called non-existent can be found in Srebrenica-related graves, according to this DNA data. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say a thing, because I, myself, did not see the list. I can trust your words, but I would need to take a look, I would need to have the time to do that, and then I could tell you. And if Dr. Brunborg did that in time for 7.661 persons, and if he said, "These are the ones that I found on the list," "These are the ones that I did not find on the list for various reasons," if he had done that in time, then I would be in a position to tell you what I think about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you stated that the more sources you have, the higher degree of reliability there is for your statistical research; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not exactly how I said it, Madam. In any profession, it is very important to be very precise. I did not say that it is important to have many sources. You can have a thousand of them, but they don't have to be good. But if you have good and reliable sources which will provide good-quality data, then obviously it is good to have more of them because your job is to produce the most reliable data possible. It is up to a professional to evaluate a source as good or not, and it's very important. The sources that I used were the ones that I considered relevant in order to obtain reliable results and data.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: In asking this question, Madam, I was actually referring precisely to your words at page 47, lines 23 and 24, but I'll go on. Now, what I'm understanding is that you're suggesting that the data gathered and collected by an internationally-recognised and neutral organisation, such as the ICRC, is possibly less reliable than, for example, the data from Ministries of Defence or offices of former warring parties, such as the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, Madam. I said something totally different. I said that a source of information coming from the BiH Army, by its quality, is the same if not even better than the sources that the OTP experts have used. I -- the way I worded my answer is not the way you say I worded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go for a moment to this ABiH list that we discussed -- that you discussed yesterday. Your basic argument for the lack of reliability of the OTP missing and dead list was, in part, based on your analysis of the ABiH list, and one of the things you noted in your report was that more than 100 persons found on both the ABiH list and the OTP list were listed as dead or missing prior to July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you provided us a few weeks ago with annex 3 to your report, where you listed by name 137 such persons from the ABiH list, that you say were listed as -- or that were listed at dead or missing prior to July 1995 on the ABiH list?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if we go now to Exhibit 3D457, and for the purposes of what I'd like to show, could we not broadcast this document, please, and if we could please take it to annex 2, which is page 5 of this document. And, Madam, just so you know what we're talking about, this is the 24 July 2008 memo by Ewa Tabeau that you discussed in your testimony, where she matched the OTP missing list with the ABiH list and then with the newest ICMP data that was obtained in July, and indeed she found even a higher number of individuals that on the ABiH list were listed at missing prior to 1995. She actually found 220. And of those 220 individuals, if you look all the way to the right, under the rubric "ICMP Grave-site, July 2008," you will see the names of grave-sites listed. In other words, of these same 220 individuals reported to be missing by the ABiH prior to 1995, 140 can be located in Srebrenica-related graves?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for all 220, but for 140. But there is another thing that is very important here. There is a number of certificates issued by the ABiH Army. There is 135 of them which has been disclosed. I will not enter into the reasons why this was done, but it is evident that the date of death was erased and tampered with. And these certificates were sent to The Hague in July of 2004. I controlled the material in February 2007. I will not try to provide any evaluation of these certificates and why they were altered. Among these certificates, I found all the persons that I named as dead, because then the names were not erased. Nothing was changed to say that the ABiH Army had sent a list to the effect that the person did not die in 2004 but in 2005. In other words, the material that I had at my disposal showed fewer persons than listed by Dr. Tabeau, but what I did is not any sort of a revision, and I don't consider that a mistake on my part. If I had had available the certificates at the time, and if I had been aware of the changes in the dates of death, then I would have had a different explanation or I would have sought an explanation. There are various explanations for that possible. For example, this could have been done in order for Mr. Jeffrey Nice to get the confirmation of the names of the soldiers who indeed were killed in 1992, 1993, 1994, or later. The letter that was returned to the demographic department of the OTP says: "At your request, we have revised the list, and we have established that the following persons did not get killed in 1994, but in 1995." This is what I saw here over the course of the past few days. There are situations in which, for example, a soldier got a certificate proving that he was a member of the BH Army from 1992 to 1994, and then again between 11 July and -- 11th of July, for one day, and that he went missing on the 11th of July. I really can't be the judge of the whole situation. The situation is possible, but what I'm saying is that this information about the revision has been in existence in the demographic department for a long time, and when I was dealing with the BH Army documents, I never knew that they existed. Nobody ever alerted me to their existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, another source that you discuss was a set of four CDs that you analysed, and they're titled "Data on Displaced Persons from Srebrenica," individual levels with names and other details. Now, do you know who compiled these four CDs?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What CDs are you talking about? Please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Madam, just a moment. In your report, at page 34, you list these documents as D000-2101 all the way to 2104, concerning lists of persons displaced from Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can't find it. You probably are quoting from the English version. The page is not the same. But when you mention displaced persons, I know what you're talking about. Those are CDs that I have received from the Defence as materials disclosed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who compiled these lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the list containing names, family names, and so on and so forth? Well, I really couldn't be able to tell you. I don't remember. I really can't remember, as I sit here, who it was. It was a long time ago when I did that, and at this moment I can't remember who the author of the lists is, but I can check. There are CDs, there are lists, and it's easy to establish who the author of those lists is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, basically you -- you find that there are 36.562 people you could locate on these four CDs as being displaced from Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke. The version that I enclosed contained 36.000 something, but the true figure is 34.457. When I arrived here, I disclosed that to the attorney-at-law, who informed you and provided you with a new CD. So 36.000 is not correct as a figure. The correct figure is 34.457 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You provided us with an annex also, indicating that 23 persons that you were able to find in this displaced persons list were also found in the OTP missing list; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just by way of example to show that it is possible, if you have the name and the date and place of birth, you can find dozens of people under the same name and with the same personal data. I have just illustrated this by singling out 23 people, and I'm not claiming that they are the same people. But they could be, according to Dr. Brunborg's methodology. In my report, I even say that specifically, that if we apply Dr. Brunborg's methodology, that we could arrive at the conclusion that they are the same people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if we could have Exhibit P0614 also not broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, on the left side is the table -- is a copy of the table that you presented to us in your table at annex 5. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And on the right side is the information showing that 13 of these 23 persons you claim overlap between the OTP list and the displaced person list are identified in Srebrenica-related graves?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what am I supposed to say? Am I supposed to confirm that these are the same persons who were displaced or should I confirm that the demographic department is sure, 100 per cent sure, that these are the same persons? I really wouldn't be able to do that. What I'm giving you is just an example. Whether they are really the same people, I don't know. It would take some more information for me to be able to tell you. What I see before me are people bearing the same name, the family name, with the same father's name, the same year of birth. Some of these people have been identified. I don't know how many of them are one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, it's rather similar to the line of questioning that Mr. Lazarevic had with you, where he was having you compare one name to another name on different lists. My question, though, is: Are you basically saying that these four CDs that you were gathering your data from are more reliable than the data collected by the ICMP and the ICRC, as gathered together by the DU or the Demographic Unit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, and this was never my guiding thought. I never assessed the reliability of the information disclosed by the OTP. I only say that there is a lot that you have to take into account if you want it to be professional, because the situation is very complex, it's anything but black and white, and there's no way you can say this is good and this is 100 per cent reliable, and the other thing is not good. So it was not my task to assess the reliability of data. I just reviewed what the OTP used and disclosed, and I just wanted to point to the complexity of the situation and the fact that you cannot adopt a one-sided approach in dealing with such a complex situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. And turning to what I hope is the final topic, do you -- do you know what the ICMP is?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know how this term is translated, and I know what this institution is doing. If you were to ask me in detail, I don't know whether I would give you accurate enough answers. So depending on the structure of your question, the brunt of your question as to what they're doing, I wouldn't be able to give you a very precise answer. But I did hear about that organisation, and I saw some of their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And you are aware, since you did have access to the data, multiple versions of the data provided to you by the Defence counsel, of the fact that ICMP is in the process of identifying, via DNA matching, identifications of people out of various mass graves?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And they have been providing the Prosecution, and as a result the Prosecution the Defence, with updated versions of lists of persons reported as missing in Srebrenica related to the Srebrenica events of July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that the Red Cross provided some information for the region of Srebrenica. In some documents, you can find information that this region comprises ten municipalities. And then the Demographic Unit did all kinds of comparisons and provided materials where it is indicated that a person has not been identified yet, has been identified, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And when you're talking about identifications, I'm assuming you're referring to this document that might have been shown to you by Defence counsel, the progress report, the newest list of missing matched together with the identifications; is that correct? And for the record, this is P003159A.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just have it for a moment to look at the front page, because I handled several lists. Yes, yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just based on their November data, you were aware that there were DNA identifications of approximately 4.300 -- well, to be exact, 4.263 Srebrenica-related victims that is said of in the introduction to that update; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there is no definition of Srebrenica. Lists that I am aware of were sent for the Srebrenica cases, I underline "cases." They pertain to the region of Srebrenica comprising ten municipalities. And the last memo, or memo that was disclosed by the Prosecution, does not speak only about identified persons, but also buried persons, and it says "3.554." Out of that 3.299, Potocari, 169 individual cases. So this is the summary, but I don't know, I think this was disclosed on the 24th of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And thank you for anticipating my next question. I was just going to bring you to this document. If I could get 3D461, please. Now, Madam, you may be aware that the way that these identifications are done is that the bone DNA samples of persons from graves are matched against blood donor samples that are collected, and there are, as has been to testified to already by Dr. Brunborg, over 20.000 such blood samples actually collected. Now, in the third row of this tracking chart for the Srebrenica cases, the number of missing individuals represented by the blood samples collected, as of - and this is an update dated July 18th, 2008 - the number of missing according to the ICMP data is 7.789 persons. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And based on just the preliminary analysis of the data that we obtained on 3 July, and this is the Excel spreadsheet data with all the names listed, we were able to just find out, and you can find that information in Dr. Tabeau's memo at 3D457, that there were at least 4.705 such individuals who were actually found on the OTP list of missing. Just back to the tracking chart for Srebrenica cases for a moment, you see that it has a DNA reports row, which is the third -- "DNA reports," it's called. It's the third row -- third title row down, and under it, it talks about individuals represented. The number of individuals represented currently, as of July 18th, 2008, according to the ICMP tracking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when mentioning figures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The number is 5.616 individuals represented. Now, I've read you all these figures rather quickly. One of the points is that based on the October data that you had at your disposal, including the progress report, there we saw that out of the 4.263 individuals that had been identified by the ICMP, 3.837 were also found on the OTP missing and dead list. That's approximately a 50 per cent overlap. And based on the new data and based on the new numbers that we have, there are, as I've already said, 4.705 persons found in the OTP list of missing against the data we received in July from the ICMP. Now, you would agree with me that these numbers are -- indicate growth, that numbers of identifications continue to grow, to rise?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, except if you want me to agree with you that the number is increasing. Well, I have no doubts as to the fact that the number of identified persons is growing, but I think that in the report that Dr. Brunborg and his associates did, it was not the purpose of this report to determine that the number is growing. The purpose was to determine that these were people who were killed in 1995. And there is a certain cut-off date. I think it's the 10th or the 11th of July. The fact is there is statistical indicia that cannot be ignored, that there is a large number of people who were killed before 1995 and are being counted as having died after the 11th of July, 1995. These are the facts, and there is certain indicia, even proof of that. And it is also a fact that the demographers, and it was their duty to do so, and the International Commission for Identification, do not specify what Srebrenica is, whether the people who were identified in the municipalities that Dr. Brunborg shows, the five municipalities, people originally from those areas, whether they are victims of Srebrenica. So from my point of view, I don't doubt that the number of people identified is growing, but the key problem is to determine when or, rather, how many of those persons who have been identified are those who cannot be linked with Srebrenica based on the date of the events in Srebrenica. How many of the people amongst those identified cannot geographically, territorially, be linked with Srebrenica and the events in Srebrenica in July? I think this is the key question. And from where I sit, as I said, there are numerous indicia as to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, is your conclusion here today that there are actually fewer individuals missing related to the fall of Srebrenica than have been identified as dead in Srebrenica by the ICMP up to date?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There seems to be a misunderstanding. What do you base your claim that this is my conclusion on, what reports, what statements I made? Maybe I am not making myself clear, and I would like me to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, it was just a simple question. I want to know whether you find that the ICMP data, the ICMP numbers, are -- don't support -- or, rather, let me start again. The individuals listed as missing by ICMP at this point in time are 7.789. It's actually a larger number than the data compiled by the OTP Demographic Unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my profession, you have to be precise. I do not challenge the fact that the ICMP quoted those figures. I said a little while ago it is very important for me to know what territory is covered. How do they define Srebrenica? They say "related to Srebrenica," is that how they phrase it? But we can define this courtroom in different ways, and let alone an area that covers several municipalities. So I am not disputing that this is the number put forward by the International Commission for Missing Persons, but I don't know what they mean when they say "Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam, you are aware of the fact that there has been testimony and there's been evidence of numbers of graves, both primary and secondary mass graves, related to Srebrenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, these graves continue to be exhumed? I don't know if you're aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This is not my area, so I haven't been following it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And as exhumations continue, more samples -- and more samples are going to the ICMP and are being tested against the 21.327 samples donated by individuals who are reporting to the ICMP that their loved ones went missing sometime after the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer the question. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is this a question or a speech? The lady's already said she has no knowledge of this. It doesn't seem to be a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
