utterances.text: Let her continue. We are getting there. I mean, let's hear the question eventually. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, Madam, basically does DNA data lie, do you know? Does it misreport?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam, I'm not a doctor, I'm not a physician. This is not my area of expertise. I have no reason to even think that they lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Next question, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Is there re-examination, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not from me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If I may, can I start right now? Thank you. I would like to go back to the document that we saw in e-court a little while ago, 3D461.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is the document that you, Professor, heard several questions by my learned colleague today. What I would like to ask you is this: When you went through all the lists that we submitted to you, as we received them from the Prosecution as part of the disclosure, could you please tell us, the ICMP lists of identified persons, do those lists contain cases or, to be quite specific, persons on those lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They list cases. What that means is that one person can be listed several times. So you have a list where a certain name with the same identification attributes appears several times because several analyses are done, so these are not persons, these are cases. And that is why there are many duplicates on those lists. So if you had a list with 5.000 something, if you get rid of all the duplicates, you get maybe 3.000, two and a half, depending on what list you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your practice, once the DNA analysis is done, once a person is identified using this analysis, is this sufficient to determine whether a person really died or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not my practice, I don't do that, but I -- based on what I heard from people and my participation in some other cases, well, they say that the process of identification ends once the relatives are invited to identify that person and to provide information that they have. That's how it ends, and it starts with the exhumation. So I'm not an expert in this area. This is what I heard from experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And have you ever seen death certificates in your practice?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my practice, I dealt with death certificates while I worked in statistics, because a death certificate is a document that is -- it's a document that is kept in perpetuity. When you enter a person into the register of deaths, there has to be a death certificate filed, and it is kept there in the archives. One copy of the death certificate goes to the statistics office, the office that employees physicians, who then, on the basis of this death certificate, determine the cause of death and so on. So this was one way in which I dealt with death certificates. The second way was when I participated in a trial being conducted before the Sarajevo Court, and then for the purposes of my analysis I received not only the identification records, but also the death certificates, so that I was able to see that there are death certificates. And I consider the death certificates to be official documents. And in my work here, I did not have an opportunity to look at the death certificates, but I didn't seek them, so I don't know whether they exist or not. It was only in early 2000, in Sarajevo, was I able to see that it is possible to obtain not only the identification records issued by ICMP, but also the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the document that we have in front of us here on the screen. Could we just scroll down a little bit. According to this document, if you look at totals, it says "Number of closed cases," and if I'm not mistaken, it says "3.554."

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this, we can then conclude that the ICMP has closed 3.554 cases to date?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And after that, the procedure to determine whether this person really -- those persons really died starts, and then the death certificate is issued. Are you aware of this procedure?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to the procedure, nobody could be entered into the death register without a death certificate, and death certificates cannot be issued before all legal and other requirements have been met. So I did come across such situations. You cannot enter anyone into the death register, and it is quite well known, it's that way all over the world. You have those register books, register of births, or register of deaths, and we also had a register of marriages. That's what we had in the former Yugoslavia. These are all documents that are kept in perpetuity, for ages, provided, of course, nothing happens, no disasters. So nobody can be entered into the registry -- register of deaths if there is no death certificate, and the death certificate must be signed by a medical doctor. There are exceptions. The Court may, if it is impossible to find the body, declare somebody dead, and pursuant to this ruling of the Court, this person can then be entered into the register of deaths.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please now have document 3D455 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear on our screen, Doctor, just for your information, this is a letter that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the federal Defence Ministry, sent on the 4th of August, 2004, to the OTP. It's about the issue that my learned friend raised in cross-examination, the soldiers who were killed before 1995. I don't want to waste our time. This is the response of the Federal Minister of Defence informing the OTP about the total of 142 members of the BH Army and other persons that are being sought about the date -- this is all about the date of their death. You have seen this document in the course of preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We received 142 certificates appended to this document?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the Defence Ministry informs the OTP that in light of the circumstances, the fact that these people were killed as they tried to cross into the BH Army-controlled territory after the capture of Srebrenica, it is very difficult to obtain verified information about the circumstances of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at 3D451 in e-court. That would be one of those certificates. Well, I don't want to look at all 142 of them. The date of this letter is the 4th of August, 2004. I would like to keep this document confidential. I don't want the public to have access to it. Professor, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is this one of those certificates, 140-odd certificates, that you inspected as you prepared for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the date is the 28th of July, 2004?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the year of birth of these people -- of this person is 1946?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On this certificate, the year of birth is listed as 1946, but such a person with this first name, last name, and father's name does not exist in the Prosecution list, the 7.661 persons. There is another person bearing the same first name, last name, and father's name, but he was born on the 7th of March, 1935. The Prosecution considered this person to have been identified and indicates that the identification was carried out. I have to stress that it's 13 years between the two years listed as years of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, I don't want to go back to this document. It's Prosecution Exhibit P3159A. It's page 91 in e-court or 87 in hard copy, so I don't want to look at it now. But, Professor, were you able to find a number of such cases as you inspected the material disclosed to us by the Prosecution in May 2008?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And does that confirm your argument about the overall findings that the Defence received?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That confirms my view and raises reasonable doubt that anything that was done must be redone in a much more careful manner, and this confirms my initial view that things were painted in black and white. Of course, the only thing where I don't have any doubts about is that the methodology that was used was no good.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You do have reasonable doubt or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt whatsoever. This methodology is not used anywhere in the world but in the demographic department of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that reasonable doubt was not being used as a legal term, but simply a term of opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so. I mean, I don't think -- anyway, I leave it to you to clarify. All right. Now, we have only got left the residues of what I brought up earlier on as preliminaries. No, Madam, we can actually dispose of her. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Excuse me, I wouldn't mind asking her a couple of questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thought no one else --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But if she would like a break now, I can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It really won't take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Otherwise, we can do this: I figured out that we may have 15 minutes, at the most, to dispose of the other issues, probably less than that; five minutes cross-examination -- redirect by Mr. Haynes. If there is no objection, we can sit a further 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Objections from the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Objections from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine, fine, no objection. Did I hear "objection"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought I heard "no objections" from the booth. No objections, yes. Okay. Now, if there is an objection, speak now. No objections. Mr. Haynes, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, I'd just like you to help me, please, with a document which I think you've only seen quite recently and which was shown to you in cross-examination by Ms. Soljan, and it's P3159A. And it might be useful if we looked at page 9 together, please. Thank you. Now, I'm really interested in you helping me and us with, as it were, the last two entries on the far right of those pages. The protocol number indicates what, according to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only rephrase what Dr. Tabeau says. I did not deal with that. In one of her reports, Dr. Tabeau says that every person is attached to protocol for identification, and these protocols exist in order to follow a person, because one person may be given two, three, or five findings, and all those are then compiled under a protocol. But I would not be able to tell you, with any degree of certainty, what a protocol is. I can only tell you that the first figures, I assume, are just the initial figures, and the last two digits are the years when the body was exhumed, and all that, if I were able to sum up what Mrs. Tabeau did, and she's the one who provides more detail of the meaning and the essence of protocols. I, myself, did not deal with that or dwell upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. But if we go to the very last column, far easier, the grave-site indicates, as you understand it, a grave-site where a body or a part of that body, which has been matched through DNA, was discovered; yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these are grave-sites, but I wouldn't be able to guarantee you that there is an indication of the match. I can tell you that this indicates that a body or parts of the body, indeed, were found, but I can't tell you whether a matching exercise was carried out and whether a match was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. But just looking at the spreadsheet, where we have no protocol and no grave-site, your understanding of that would mean we've not found a part of that body anywhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with you, but I cannot be 100 per cent sure that that would be correct. But I assume that if there were any document, it would probably be entered in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I just want you to look down at one, two, three, four, five, six -- the seventh entry down on the grave-site list. I think it reads "Seher."

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- can you repeat the name? Number 7 or line 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's line 7 if you follow the grave-sites. Yes, I'm terribly sorry, this should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine, then let's not broadcast it. Have you been broadcasting it? We haven't. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Count the grave-site names rather than the names of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Not the lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have counted them, and I have found there that this is a grave-site named "Seher."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you come across that name in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you another document that you were shown by Mr. Lazarevic, and I've got this in hard copy. So if somebody could put it on the ELMO. And I'm afraid I must confess, I will have to beg assistance as to whether this has a 65 ter number from, perhaps, Ms. Cmeric. Just show it to her, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's a document that Ms. Soljan handed out this morning. It's the thinner of the two documents, if the Bench have it. And I just wonder whether the first sheet of that document can be placed on the ELMO, please, so we can all see. Again, please don't broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, would you, with me, Dr. Radovanovic, go down to an entry relating to a man called Alic, Beriz, whose father's name was Bekto?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document that you have just shown me; is that where you want me to look for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the family name, kindly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's Alic. His first name is Beriz, and his father's name apparently was Bekto. And can we go across to where he was buried, please? Giving the amount I'm actually putting onto the record, this better be in private session, not just not broadcast, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Radovanovic, your testimony comes to an end, and first and foremost I wish to thank you for having come over and for having stayed with us all these days to give your entire testimony. On behalf of everyone present here, I also wish to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's start with the documents. Let's get rid of them. Mr. Lazarevic -- sorry, not Mr. Lazarevic. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am just receiving a message, a mail message from my assistants, that they are just in the process of completing the list. It will take them another ten minutes, if I may ask your indulgence and allow them to complete that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do the documents last, then. Let's do the documents last, and let's go through the so-called preliminaries. The Drago Nikolic motion, yesterday's motion seeking leave to add one witness to his Rule 65 ter lists -- yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm trying to see you both. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, no objection. Is there any objection from the other Defence teams? No. So permission is granted. We are deciding the motion orally by granting leave, there being no opposition. The Nikolic two motions seeking protective measures. Let's take them one by one, please. One moment until I find ... yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can address those, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first, one motion requesting protective measures and delayed disclosures of the identity of Witness 3DW10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've reached agreement with our friends, no objection to the protective measures sought in that motion. And we've spoken on the name, they have agreed to disclose to us after the break so that there's no disagreement on this motion. It's the week of the 18th of August the name will be disclosed to us, and no objection to voice and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So if my colleague agrees with me, the best way to go about it is not to decide it now. We'll wait to see that this has, indeed, taken place, and then we'll declare the motion moot. Okay, is that agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The other motion, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agree. And then the protective measures will be issued, then, after the recess. And then there is the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- motion relating to witnesses W5, W6, W7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I also believe 29 is in there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and 29. Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think with that one, we're not ready to give a final answer. I can talk to my friends some more after the break, but we will file something before the close of business tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think there is no urgency, in any case. It can wait until we return. We still have a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we may reach an agreement. I'll talk to my friend. I just didn't have time to talk about all the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That leaves us with the Beara issue. We have gone through the response filed yesterday night by the Beara Defence team. Do you wish to address the Chamber, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can very briefly, Your Honour, although I think the pleadings speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Can I just direct you, as regards the list of exhibits, I think there isn't much --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to thank my friends for providing that and say that's no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. As regards compliance or otherwise with Rule 67(A)(ii), do you have anything to start after reading what Mr. Beara has stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- namely, that they don't have any further statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what they say, Your Honour, is that they don't have any further signed witness statements, and what our request would be, if those -- if they have statements which are unsigned of witnesses who they intend to call viva voce that have not been provided, that they be provided to us straight away. I don't think signing or not signing should be a -- I don't want to say a way to get around a rule, but a factor. When the witnesses come and are proofed, if they have -- the signed statement can be provided to us, and if there are errors or changes, then that will be in the proofing note. But if we can get the information now, that's what we request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that we were quite clear, if we had possession of any such statements, we would give them to him, with the exception of several witnesses that the Prosecution has interviewed or have given other testimony in other ICTY proceedings here. We can provide that to them, if that's what they really wish for, but I think they have them, because they've provided them to us from time to time. But we're not in possession of any statements, signed or otherwise. We do have counsel notes. One of our legal assistants had passed away. I do have some of his notes, not all. We are going to the field the entire during the break in order to obtain more information from each of the remaining witnesses that we have. And as I've set forth in my motion, we will, immediately upon obtaining any such statement, send that to them, as well as any other information that they deem relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Having heard that, would you be happy with not having a decision at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, my friend's told me he doesn't have any more statements taken by them of any witnesses, signed or unsigned, and if that's the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. And as regards the first part of his response, namely, the summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we stand by our motion. We've compared the summaries attached to the filing from last night to the summaries which have previously been provided and they haven't been changed at all from the motion which we submitted a few days ago, so we stand by our pleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't there a possibility that you meet tomorrow - we are not sitting - and you discuss this? When we were having the same problem with the Popovic Defence team --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- a meeting which lasted barely half an hour helped solve all the problems to mutual satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, my view is no. I've met with them, I met with him and Mr. Thayer a long time ago. We've been e-mailing. We have sat down and spoken, as Mr. McCloskey said, before we filed this pleading. We have tried. We feel we need a court order. I do not think it would be profitable in the least, frankly, based on past efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a question of that we agree to disagree. We've met not only with Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Thayer, but I think with Mr. Elderkin and Mr. McCloskey for time and time again, and we've met for a very long time. They seem to agree on some points, but it's not enough for them. I think if we read the rule, and I think quite frankly if you look at two, if I can just highlight, or even three of the witnesses out of the remaining 17 and just compared their 65 ter list summaries of that witness with what the witness said in an interview to them, what the witness said during his testimony in another case, and we met with the witness, admittedly, on one occasion to confirm that which he said in an interview to the OTP. If they need more information than that, I truly cannot provide that to them. I think they're really being unreasonable on this point. I strongly believe that our summaries are more than sufficient and in compliance with the Rule, and I would ask the Court to reject -- if they're not even willing to sit down, to reject their requests on these 65 ter summaries that they're requesting. I think that they have more than enough information. It provides them the factual backdrop, it gives them notice of the witnesses. They've clearly not been prejudiced when any of the witness that have come forward. Even Witness who was 2DW007, Mr. Mrkovic, they had his intercepts. They failed to provide that to us in a timely basis. They've had it for a long time. If the Prosecution truly believes they are being prejudiced in any way, they could have, and, in my opinion, should have filed a motion immediately after May 1st 2008, not wait during my Defence case, not wait at the eve of a break. They could have requested and met with us and made that statement well before, as the Court, I think, suggested to them when they were dealing with the Popovic matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, that's just why there's no point in meeting. He thinks his 65 ter summaries are fully adequate, even ones which say things like he'll discuss an even in 1992. He thinks he doesn't need to provide -- tell us what the witness will say, if the witness is given an interview. There is really nothing left to discuss and we just hope for a ruling. And I don't want to take time, but we have been prejudiced by these delayed disclosures or lack of -- complete lack of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one last point, if I may, Mr. President. We have amended them and we have provided them additional information. It's just not adequate. We've given them the names that they've requested, the date of birth, the father's name, all the information that they've had in their own database and in the database that we utilise together. We are sticking with our summaries on this issue. If they really want to know what he said about 1992, I'm sure it will draw an objection. I think really what they want, I can go back and call this witness this afternoon. If they want to know what event, I quite frankly don't know what he's going to say about 1992, but I'm sure it involves Bratunac and possibly and Mr. Deronjic, which they're very familiar with. But if they really need that information and they're being prejudiced because of -- a witness is going to say something in 1992 [sic], I'll provide it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are unnecessarily taking a very rigid position, both of you, we have spent hours going through the summaries and the complaints of the Prosecution to see whether they were -- and also because it's not exactly easy to establish criteria on the basis of which you can decide whether a summary is adequate or sufficient or insufficient, but while I say you're taking a very rigid position unnecessarily, I mean it. There is, for example, in relation to Witness C. Majovanovic [phoen] one of the Prosecution complaints was information should have been -- more information on the facts underlying the witness's alibi testimony, such as attending Beara's birthday party and other facts relating to the 1990 episodes of how Beara adhered to JNA policy of calming down ethnic tensions, I'm sure you have more details than this laconic description of what this witness is supposed to be testifying again. Again, in relation to Bojan Subotic, Bojan Subotic, in your summary you have: "Witness will also testify about an event from 1992." And no one knows what this event is. You don't need criteria at this point in time to establish whether the summary, as far as this goes, is sufficient or not. Don't you think that the Prosecution are not entitled to know what event you are talking about or this witness would be talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you do make a good point with respect to Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning two -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll clarify that point right there, so they can have a restful vacation. We'll withdraw that aspect. I won't lead any evidence of this witness with respect to events leading to 1992. I did suggest to meet with them. I'm not taking a rigid approach, with all due respect. They refuse to because they're not satisfied with whatever we give them, with respect, other than if I depose and have a court reporter there and if they're present during the sessions with the witnesses. With respect to Mr. Subotic, I think really his testimony will relate to the other aspects other than 1992, so I will orally here amend that 65 ter summary. And if that was their concern, since they cite it, I think we have an agreement that the rest of them should be adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is what I mean. It's like pulling teeth. I don't know the amount of times we have asked for that information about 1992. Mr. Ostojic is trying to act as though this has just come up. We've asked for that before. We've asked in e-mails, and we haven't gotten it. You've been able to get something, Your Honours. We're not, on our own. And to be clear, we stand by our pleading, and I ask him to correct his 65 ter summaries and submit them immediately or provide the relief we sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I was on trial with not nine lawyers or eight lawyers but two lawyers, so with all due respect I did not find in my priority list that this was that critical and that it would prejudice them. Had I known that it was that important, and I do apologise to them, I should have responded to them. But I didn't believe when they requested that an event in 1992 is that important that it may cause the Prosecution prejudice. That was my decision and I take full responsibility for that. But I had witnesses here under some adverse circumstances. We tried to do the best we could. I think accomplished the guidelines that the Court set forth for that. I will address that issue with my learned friend if that's really his concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, we have to close down within the next three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last point. I mean, you can see how strongly Mr. Ostojic, I believe, is arguing on behalf of his client, and we understand that. I have been facilitating this process the whole time, and I can tell you it's reached an end. What's happening here is my team and my lawyers are getting tied down by this, and it's taking away time. We're stuck protecting the Srebrenica area, when we want to be in Trnovo, and it's something that we need to get on with the case and not go into this constant reframe that's not going anywhere. He's strongly defending his client. In our view, we need a court order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am concerned, because you might recall, when a motion was filed in relation to the Popovic Defence 65 ter summaries, I jumped into the ring on that one, because I feared that this would be a procedure that was used to make even more difficult the process of presenting your case. And we compromised that, and perhaps I and several others here misunderstood the agreement we had, but I perceived there to be an agreement that the Prosecution would not use this procedure again. And there is still, as it were, relief sought in my cross-motion that any further applications for amplified 65 ter summaries was to be made by a date that we have now passed, and so I have some sympathy for Mr. Ostojic in his impassioned plea that this comes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what I really want to know is: Are we to assume that we must press on for you to rule that any further requests must be made within a limited time, or is there an agreement that this turn will not be used against the rest of us who are waiting to present our cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have to break. Either bring it to an end here -- let's break for five minutes, until they change the tapes, and conclude this story. Five minutes. You can stay here, actually. I mean, and in the meantime Judge Kwon and myself will have a chance to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll try to be as brief as possible. We primarily feel that you should help us in your own interests, not just the Beara team at the moment but also the others too, to avoid putting us in a position where we have to decide these issues. And I don't need to say much. I think you should all know why. We do understand that everyone is used to his or her own domestic system. In my country, for example, you would only be required, before the trial, to indicate the purpose of the testimony of each particular witness that you intend to bring over, and you have to indicate the entire list of witnesses you intend to bring over, but that's about it. You don't furnish any summaries at all. But we have our system here. I do know what the system is and I can quite understand that sometimes it's difficult to adapt, but we have our own system here, and our own system requires that intelligible summaries which are sufficient on the face of it are to be provided. We think that the best way to go about it at the present moment, also in the hope that the next couple of weeks will help you relax a little bit and approach this matter in a more serene way, is for you to sit down together, identify who the first ten witnesses are going to be after the break, find out whether, in relation to any of those ten witnesses, there is still an outstanding dispute between you as to the sufficiency or otherwise of the summary, and sort out those for the time being. We have gone through all the summaries, and we don't believe that it should be difficult. However, to help you, we also are in a position to indicate to you that although we agree with some of the objections of the Prosecution, in other words, we think that more information is warranted, there are some witnesses where we are satisfied that sufficient information has been given, and we are going to give you the names so that you will have this clear on your table when you meet and discuss. First of all, there were two witnesses that there seemed to be an agreement that the information provided was insufficient, but it's already on record that the Beara team promised to add more information. We are talking of - I will just give numbers - 2DW24, 2DW21, and 2DPW20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless any of these is being dropped, Judge Kwon is telling me that in your latest filing you have indicated that you are dropping 2DW24, but, anyway, that's up to you. Now, we consider that the summaries relating to the following witnesses, 2DW17, 2DW18, 2DW34, 2DW63, 2DWPW1, we are satisfied with the summaries provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less it. I mean, we had reached these conclusions, although we are not deciding the motion prior to seeing Beara's response, of course, which we will study further. So basically now you know where we wouldn't expect any further developments. But in the case of other summaries, other witnesses, we suggest you deal first in an open manner and in a positive way with the ones that we will be dealing with soon after the recess, and then we decide, if necessary, about the others. But as we don't know exactly who you intend to bring over starting on the 25th of August, now that we are not sitting -- yeah, but we are not sitting now on the 20th, 21st and 22nd, so I wouldn't know, Mr. Ostojic, whether you would need to revise your strategy and your list. I will leave that in your hands, because we wouldn't interfere. But having said that, once you know exactly who, it's easy to sit down with Mr. Nicholls or whoever, see exactly what else they do require. At the end of the day, they are not asking for information that is going to compromise your case. I mean, some of it is so neutral, and it only helps. I mean, at the end of the day it could help you as well. Do you wish to comment on this proposed approach or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We'll, of course, follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When are you leaving town, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I -- and I've set my schedule. I'm meeting with various witnesses here Friday and Tuesday, and then I'm leaving for Vienna, and then Dubrovnik to meet a witness that they know about, then Tuzla and Sarajevo. So I will be on -- in the field throughout this entire two and a half weeks. And as I said, I offered that I'd give them -- once I sit down with these witnesses, I'll give them what information they deem appropriate. But I will be here -- Friday night I have a meeting with an expert that's here in the Netherlands, so I could meet Saturday morning as early as they'd like, or Sunday in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our hope is that by the time we meet again on the 25th of August, this dispute would have whittled down to nothing or little. All right. So I wish you a nice break. Oh, yes, we still have the exhibits. I forgot those. Ms. Nikolic, thank you for reminding me. We were too anxious to make you come to an agreement. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My assistants have provided me with a list and have provided the list to all the parties and the Chamber, so this is the list that you have in front of you. But I need to provide an explanation here. The quantity of documents, the number of documents, relates to the footnotes in Professor Radovanovic's report, and some of the documents are documents that were used in court during her examination-in-chief and the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from the other Defence teams? They are all admitted. Mr. Ostojic, do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the -- Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have nine documents to tender into evidence. A list was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that I would like to mention in this respect, that the last three documents, we believe that they should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. They are admitted, and the last three documents will remain under seal. So I wish you all a nice break and that you will return full of energy when we resume on the 25th of August. Thank you.
